screens.title: Scaling Fabric Networks
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this chapter you will learn how to make a Hyperledger Fabric network grow reliably as user demand and transaction volume increase. We begin with a practical distinction: vertical scaling means increasing C P U, memory, or disk for an existing node, while horizontal scaling means adding more peers, orderers, or CAs. Both approaches are useful; vertical scaling gives quick capacity gains but hits limits and can create single points of failure, while horizontal scaling favors resilience and distribution. You will see concrete steps for adding a peer to a channel and for expanding a Raft ordering cluster. We also cover sharding with multiple channels, which partitions workload so independent ledgers process transactions in parallel, and cloud deployment concerns such as persistent storage, managed Kubernetes, networking, and monitoring. A short hands-on activity shows the test-network addOrg3 script and the verification commands you will run. As you move through the lesson, notice trade-offs: throughput versus synchronization overhead, and resilience versus configuration complexity. By the end you should be able to choose where to invest resources, how to add instances safely, and how to design channels to increase throughput without breaking application semantics. Consider what would be harder to change later: a single oversized node or a channel design that prevents sharding? That question will guide your design choices.

Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Scaling Fabric Networks
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Scaling Fabric Networks

Learn when to grow a node versus when to grow the network, how to add peers and Raft orderers, how channels shard work for throughput, and what to plan for in cloud deployments.

Explore Key Topics
Vertical Scaling
Quickly increase CPU, RAM, or storage for a node to boost capacity.
Horizontal Scaling
Add peers, orderers, or CAs to distribute load and improve fault tolerance.
Sharding (Channels)
Partition workloads using multiple channels to increase parallel throughput.
Coming up: hands-on peer add, Raft expansion, and cloud deployment checklist.
Concept Map
Capacity, Resilience, and Partitioning
In this lesson
Tip: plan for both scaling types and map them to the component's role — stateful stores need persistent volumes, consensus needs odd Raft nodes, and channels enable sharding.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this segment we set clear, measurable objectives so you know what competence looks like. First, you will be able to distinguish between vertical and horizontal scaling strategies for each Fabric component and explain the trade-offs in terms of throughput, availability, and operational complexity. For example, you should be able to explain why a CA may remain a vertical candidate initially while peers are scaled horizontally. Second, you will learn how to implement horizontal scaling by adding peers and organizations to a running Fabric network. This includes registration with the CA, generating MSP materials, starting the new peer, and ensuring it joins channels and synchronizes its state database. Both objectives stress practical verification steps so you can show a new peer's block height matches existing peers. These skills matter because scaling decisions affect cost, resilience, and the ability to meet SLAs. Expect to practice these steps using the test-network scripts and to reason about when to choose vertical upgrades instead of adding instances. By the end you will have both the how-to steps and the judgement criteria for production deployments.

First, you will understand how to scale the ordering service by adding Raft nodes, including why odd-numbered quorums matter and how adding nodes increases fault tolerance while raising consensus overhead. screens.title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling — Core Definition
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the two fundamental scaling axes and see what they mean for Fabric. Vertical scaling is increasing the resources of an existing server or container: more C P U cores, more R A M, faster disks. For a Fabric peer or orderer, vertical scaling raises single-node capacity, allowing heavier endorsement workloads or faster block processing on that node. However, vertical scaling eventually hits hardware or cost ceilings and concentrates risk: if that node fails, its services are unavailable unless other redundant nodes exist. Horizontal scaling is adding more instances of a component: more peers in an organization, additional orderers in a Raft cluster, or more CA replicas. In Fabric horizontal scaling distributes load and improves fault tolerance because requests can be balanced across instances. In practice, Fabric favors horizontal scaling where possible: peers can endorse and serve queries in parallel, Raft nodes can be added to tolerate failures, and multiple CAs can be deployed behind a load balancer. A common misconception is that simply adding peers will always increase throughput without costs: more peers increase gossip and state synchronization overhead and can add endorsement policy complexity. A concrete example: adding peer0. org3 to a channel spreads endorsement load for read-heavy queries, but you must ensure it synchronizes the ledger with existing peers before serving clients. Takeaway: match the axis to the component's role — use vertical improvements for input and output-bound storage or temporary boosts, and horizontal expansion for sustained, distributed demand.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Vertical vs Horizontal
Core Concept

Vertical and Horizontal Scaling

Precise definitions for Fabric. Understand where each approach applies and what trade-offs to expect in operation.

Vertical scaling
  • Increase CPU, RAM, or disk for an existing node.
  • Fast to apply, limited by hardware and risk of single failure.
Horizontal scaling
  • Add more peers, orderers, or CA instances to distribute work.
  • Improves availability but adds sync and consensus overhead.
Key Takeaway

Match scaling type to component role: use vertical for storage-bound nodes and horizontal for distributed workloads and resilience.

Analogy
Single big truck
Carries more but if it breaks, everything stops — like a vertically scaled node.
Many small trucks
Work in parallel and still deliver if a few fail — like horizontal peers or orderers.
Common mistake

Assuming adding peers always increases throughput. More peers increase synchronization and endorsement policy complexity; design and verify carefully.

screens.title: Scaling Peers: Add a New Peer to an Organization
screens.narratorSegment: Scaling peers means adding new instances so endorsement and query load distributes. The practical sequence has clear stages: identity provisioning, crypto material generation, container start, channel join, and verification. Start by registering and enrolling the new peer identity with your Fabric CA. That produces a cryptographic identity and MSP folder. Next, create or copy the peer's TLS artifacts and ensure the CORE_PEER_* environment variables describe the new instance. When the peer process starts, it advertises itself and participates in gossip. Before exposing it to clients, the peer must obtain the channel genesis or latest config block and run peer channel join. That causes the peer to request missing blocks from existing peers and sync its ledger via gossip. After joining, verify synchronization by running peer channel getinfo to compare block height to a known good peer. A concrete example: adding peer0. org3 to mychannel requires setting CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID to Org3MSP, pointing CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH to Org3 Admin MSP, and setting CORE_PEER_ADDRESS to the peer's endpoint, then running peer channel join -b mychannel. block. A common misconception is that a newly started peer will immediately serve queries; it will not reliably do so until its state database and ledger are synchronized. Final takeaway: follow the sequence and always verify block height and sample chaincode queries before routing production traffic.

keyIdea.title: Peer scaling checklist
keyIdea.text: Register identity, prepare MSP and TLS, start peer, join channel, and verify ledger sync before serving client traffic.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Add Peer Process
Steps
  1. Register and enroll peer identity with the CA to create MSP.
  2. Prepare TLS certificates and set CORE_PEER_* environment variables.
  3. Start peer container/process so it joins gossip and is discoverable.
  4. Fetch the channel genesis or latest config block and run peer channel join.
  5. Verify ledger synchronization and chaincode queries before serving traffic.
Misconception
A freshly started peer is not ready until it catches up; always verify block height and test chaincode responses.
Concrete Example (terminal-style)
export CORE_PEER_TLS_ENABLED=true
export CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID="Org3MSP"
export CORE_PEER_TLS_ROOTCERT_FILE=${PWD}/organizations/peerOrganizations/org3.example.com/peers/peer0.org3.example.com/tls/ca.crt
export CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH=${PWD}/organizations/peerOrganizations/org3.example.com/users/Admin@org3.example.com/msp
export CORE_PEER_ADDRESS=localhost:11051

peer channel fetch 0 mychannel.block -o localhost:7050 --tls --cafile ${PWD}/organizations/ordererOrganizations/example.com/orderers/orderer.example.com/msp/tlscacerts/tlsca.example.com-cert.pem
peer channel join -b mychannel.block
peer channel getinfo -c mychannel
Key Takeaway

Follow the sequence strictly and perform verification before routing clients to the new peer.

screens.title: Hands-on: Using addOrg3.sh in test-network
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through the test-network addOrg3 script conceptually so you understand what it automates and what you should check afterwards. The addOrg3. sh script generates crypto material for the new organization, creates an Org3 definition file, updates the channel configuration to include the new organization, and starts the peer0. org3 and CLI containers. In practice, the script runs many discrete steps: it calls cryptogen or Fabric CA tooling to create MSP folders, it prepares a channel configuration delta to add Org3MSP as a member of the Application group, and it submits a config update transaction signed by an admin from an existing organization. After the config update is applied, the script starts the Org3 containers and often joins the peer to the channel automatically. When you run the script in a lab, verify three outcomes: first, that the new organization appears in the channel configuration keys; second, that peer0. org3 successfully joined the channel and synchronized its ledger; third, that any required chaincode is installed or that you can query the ledger from Org3. A common pitfall is assuming the script completed successfully without inspecting logs; always check the config fetch decode output or run jq on the decoded config to confirm Org3MSP presence. Final guidance: treat the script as a time-saver but keep manual verification steps in your deployment checklist.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › addOrg3.sh Walkthrough
What the script automates
  • Generate crypto material and MSP for Org3.
  • Create the Org3 channel definition and config update envelope.
  • Submit the channel config update and start Org3 containers.
  • Optionally join the peer to the channel and start a CLI for verification.
Verification checklist
  1. Fetch and decode channel config; confirm Org3MSP key appears.
  2. Confirm peer0.org3 joined and block height matches others.
  3. Run a chaincode query to verify state synchronization.
Terminal recap
# Bring test-network up
cd fabric-samples/test-network
./network.sh down
./network.sh up createChannel -ca

# Add Org3 using provided helper
./addOrg3/addOrg3.sh up -c mychannel

# Verify Org3 presence by decoding channel config
peer channel fetch config config_block.pb -o localhost:7050 --tls --cafile ...
configtxlator proto_decode --input config_block.pb --type common.Block --output config_block.json
jq '.data.data[0].payload.data.config.channel_group.groups.Application.groups | keys' config_block.json
Tip: inspect script logs and the config decode output; scripted automation should be validated, not assumed.

screens.title: Gossip and Ledger Synchronization
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding gossip and ledger synchronization is essential when you add peers. Fabric's gossip protocol is the mechanism peers use to discover each other and replicate ledger blocks and state updates. When a new peer joins a channel it does not have the full ledger; it requests missing blocks after fetching the channel genesis or config block. Existing peers supply blocks through a combination of peer-to-peer block transfers and state transfer mechanisms. The new peer will replay those blocks to rebuild its chain and update its state database. A concrete example: after running peer channel join, the peer will query peers that have the blocks and receive them over the gossip protocol until its block height matches the channel. A common misconception is assuming ledger sync is instantaneous; large ledgers or slow network links can make synchronization take significant time, and peers must be monitored until their block height is consistent. Operationally, ensure the new peer has access to persistent storage sized for the ledger and that firewalls allow gossip ports. Key checks include peer channel getinfo to compare heights and performing a chaincode query to confirm expected state. Takeaway: gossip enables scaling peers but requires planning for synchronization time and network capacity to avoid false readiness assumptions.

keyIdea.text: Peers sync via gossip and block transfer; verify block heights and test chaincode after join before marking a peer ready.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Gossip & Sync
How it works

Gossip is peer-to-peer replication. New peers fetch config blocks and then request missing blocks from peers until they reach the latest height.

Checks
  • peer channel getinfo — compare block heights.
  • chaincode query — confirm state data is available.
  • peer logs — watch for block transfer activity and errors.
Common mistake
Marking a peer as ready immediately after container start without waiting for ledger catch-up.
Example verification
# After joining
peer channel getinfo -c mychannel
# Compare heights across peers; they should match
peer chaincode query -C mychannel -n basic -c '{"Args":["GetAllAssets"]}'
Why it matters

Ensuring ledger sync avoids serving stale responses and prevents peers from returning inconsistent results to clients.

screens.title: Scaling the Ordering Service (Raft)
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric's Raft ordering service is a crash-fault-tolerant consensus mechanism where ordering nodes form a cluster that provides block ordering and consensus. Horizontal scaling of Raft involves adding consenters (orderer nodes) to the cluster. A practical rule is to use an odd number of nodes — three, five, or seven — so the cluster can tolerate floor(n/2) failures while still achieving quorum. Adding nodes increases resilience: the cluster can survive more node failures without losing liveness. However, there is a trade-off: each additional node increases the communication and replication overhead required for consensus, which can affect latency, especially under high load. To add a Raft node you must generate its crypto material, fetch the latest channel config, add the new consenter entry to the config, and submit an update so other orderers accept the new member. After the config update, start the new orderer so it joins the cluster. Misconception to avoid: more orderers always improves throughput. In many cases the bottleneck is ordering throughput per channel and the increased consensus traffic can raise latency. A concrete example: expanding from three to five nodes increases tolerated failures from one to two, but you should test latency impacts. Takeaway: expand Raft to improve fault tolerance, but measure consensus overhead and align node count with your availability and latency requirements.

keyIdea.text: Use odd-numbered Raft clusters to increase fault tolerance, and weigh added consensus overhead against the need for improved resilience.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Raft Ordering
How Raft scales
Raft ordering clusters increase fault tolerance by adding consenters. Use odd numbers to maintain quorum and tolerate failures without losing liveness.
Steps to add a node
  1. Generate orderer crypto material for the new node.
  2. Fetch and decode the current channel config.
  3. Add the new node's consenter info to the config and submit the update.
  4. Start the new orderer and verify cluster membership.
Trade-offs
More nodes improve fault tolerance but increase consensus messaging and may raise latency; validate with load testing.
Example
Moving from 3 to 5 orderers increases tolerated failures from one to two. Perform a config update to add consenters and then start the new orderer so it replicates blocks and participates in leader election.
Common misconception

More orderers always increase throughput — not necessarily. Ordering bottlenecks and quorum costs can limit gains.

screens.title: Steps to Add a Raft Node (Conceptual Commands)
screens.narratorSegment: Adding a Raft orderer is an operational process with careful sequencing. Begin by generating the new orderer's cryptographic material — its TLS and MSP — using your chosen tooling. Next, fetch the latest channel configuration block from a trusted orderer and decode it to JSON. Prepare a config delta that adds the new consenter entry under the Orderer section, including its host, port, and TLS root certificate. Sign and submit the config update using the required administrative signatures from consenting organizations. After the network accepts the updated config, start the new orderer process with the generated crypto material so it can join the cluster and participate in leader election. Throughout this sequence, monitor logs for errors and confirm replication of blocks to the new node. Remember a practical misconception: you cannot simply point an orderer at an existing cluster and expect it to join without performing the channel config update; the cluster must explicitly include the new consenter. A sample conceptual command flow highlights the steps but not exact CLI syntax because implementations vary: generate crypto, fetch config, modify JSON to add consenter, create update envelope, sign and submit, then start orderer. Final takeaway: treat ordering changes as configuration surgery — prepare backups and validate cluster behavior under load after the change.

keyIdea.text: Generate crypto, update channel config with new consenter, submit signed update, then start the new orderer and verify replication.

Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Add Raft Node
Conceptual command flow
# 1. Generate crypto for new orderer (TLS and MSP)
# 2. Fetch current channel config and decode to JSON
# 3. Add new consenter info to Orderer section
# 4. Create a config update envelope and sign
# 5. Submit the config update
# 6. Start the new orderer and verify replication

Operational checks
  • Confirm updated config lists the new consenter entry.

  • Run connectivity and latency checks — consensus traffic can reveal bottlenecks.
Warning

Changing orderer membership affects cluster quorum; perform during maintenance windows and validate backups.

screens.title: Scaling Certificate Authorities (CAs)
screens.narratorSegment: Certificate Authorities manage identities and are vital for secure operations. A single CA instance can serve many organizations in a small deployment, but for production you should plan for high availability and load balancing. Fabric CA servers support configuration in front of a load balancer and can share a database backend so multiple CA instances present a single logical service. When scaling CAs horizontally, ensure the backing database supports concurrent access and backups. Vertical scaling is sometimes used for a CA during quick growth to improve response times, but it leaves a central point of failure unless replicated. Practically, you might deploy multiple CA replicas behind a load balancer and use a managed database service that provides automated backups and multi-AZ redundancy. A misconception is treating CA scaling the same as peers: while peers replicate ledgers and can be added progressively, CA scaling requires careful handling of signing keys and database consistency. Example operational steps include configuring a shared database, deploying two or more CA instances with sticky sessions disabled, and verifying enrollment responses from different replicas. Takeaway: make CAs highly available with redundant instances and robust storage, and include CA health in your restoration playbook because identity data is critical for recovery.

Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Scaling CAs
High Availability

Deploy multiple CA instances with a shared, durable database backend and load balancing to avoid having a single identity service failure point.

Practical steps
  • Configure CA replicas to use a common DB with strong consistency.
  • Load balance enrollment requests and monitor latency and errors.
  • Protect signing keys and include them in backup/restore plans.
Misconception

Treating CA scaling like peer population growth is risky; identity services require consistent signing and careful key management.

Key Takeaway

screens.title: Sharding with Multiple Channels
screens.narratorSegment: Sharding in Fabric is achieved by using multiple channels, where each channel maintains its own independent ledger and ordering. This approach enables parallel transaction processing because transactions on one channel do not contend with those on another channel's ordering pipeline. The key to effective sharding is logical partitioning: identify domains or data sets that can operate independently. For example, a supply chain network can separate raw-material tracking and finished-goods distribution into different channels so each set of transactions is ordered and endorsed independently. Implementation requires careful design: which organizations join which channels, how chaincode is deployed per channel, and how client applications route transactions to the appropriate channel. A common pitfall is failing to plan for cross-channel workflows; Fabric does not provide native cross-channel chaincode invocation, so cross-domain interactions require off-chain coordination or specialized application logic. A concrete scenario: partition by geography — na-channel, eu-channel, asia-channel — then route transactions based on asset location. Benefits include increased overall throughput and reduced contention, but trade-offs are added operational complexity, more ledgers to manage, and potential data duplication. Takeaway: use channels as a sharding mechanism when domains are separable and design cross-channel interactions explicitly at the application layer.

keyIdea.text: Use separate channels for independent domains to shard transaction load, but plan for cross-channel coordination and operational overhead.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Sharding with Channels
Concept

Separate channels, separate ledgers

Channels provide independent ordering and ledger storage, letting you partition transactions to increase parallel throughput.

Design considerations:
  • Map business domains to channels where possible.
  • Decide organization membership per channel.
  • Deploy chaincode per channel and route clients accordingly.
Example
Create na-channel, eu-channel, and asia-channel and route transactions by asset region. Each channel's ordering and endorsement pipelines run independently, increasing total throughput.
Common pitfall
Neglecting cross-channel interactions; Fabric does not provide native cross-channel chaincode calls, so plan offline aggregation or application-level coordination.
Key Takeaway

Channels are an effective sharding tool when domains are separable and you accept the operational trade-offs.

screens.title: Managed Kubernetes for Fabric
screens.narratorSegment: Managed Kubernetes services simplify running containerized Fabric components by handling node lifecycle, service discovery, and many operational primitives. Using AKS, EKS, or GKE allows you to deploy peers, orderers, and CAs as pods, benefit from Kubernetes Services for internal traffic, and use Horizontal Pod Autoscalers for stateless components. However, Fabric components are stateful and need persistent volumes for ledgers and state databases. Plan for persistent volume claims with adequate IOPS and backup strategies. Also prepare node pools with appropriate VM sizes for C P U and memory needs, and use pod affinity or anti-affinity to distribute peers across availability zones. Managed Kubernetes also provides native integrations for logging and monitoring; connect Fabric logs to the cloud's monitoring stack for alerts on latency, block processing times, and storage utilization. A common misconception is that Kubernetes alone handles all scaling automatically; many Fabric components require manual configuration, persistent storage provisioning, and careful stateful set definitions. Example action items: define StatefulSets for peers with PVCs, configure NetworkPolicies to limit traffic to necessary ports, and use readiness probes that check block height or chaincode health. Takeaway: managed Kubernetes reduces operational burden but does not eliminate planning for persistent storage, network security, and stateful workload behavior.

keyIdea.text: Use managed Kubernetes for orchestration, but explicitly provision persistent volumes, pod distribution, and readiness checks for Fabric stateful services.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Managed Kubernetes
Why use managed K8s
  • Simplifies orchestration of containers and service discovery.
  • Supports autoscaling, health checks, and rolling updates.
  • Integrates with cloud logging and monitoring systems.
Plan for stateful workloads with StatefulSets and persistent volumes. Define readiness probes that ensure a peer's ledger is sufficiently synced before accepting traffic.
Operational checklist
  • Provision PVCs with IOPS targets and backups for ledgers and state DBs.
  • Use pod anti-affinity to spread peers across zones.
  • Configure NetworkPolicies and monitor pod resource usage and logs.
Misconception

Kubernetes autoscaling cannot automatically handle ledger synchronization or consensus reconfiguration; these are operational concerns you must design for.

screens.title: Storage, Networking, and Monitoring Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: When scaling Fabric in the cloud, persistent storage, networking, and monitoring are the three pillars that determine operational reliability. Persistent storage ensures ledger and state databases survive pod restarts and node failures; choose cloud volumes with the required IOPS and throughput, and plan for scheduled backups. Under-provisioned storage is a common cause of performance problems and needs capacity planning against expected ledger growth. Networking is critical: configure VPCs, subnets, and security groups so Fabric components communicate securely with minimal latency; gossip and ordering traffic needs low-latency links to avoid consensus slowdowns. High-availability demands distributing peers and orderers across availability zones and carefully setting network routing and firewall rules. Observability completes the picture: integrate Fabric logs and metrics into cloud monitoring solutions to surface block processing time, endorsement latency, and storage utilization. Without monitoring, bottlenecks can remain hidden until users are impacted. A practical example is using Azure AKS with managed disks for PVCs, network policies to isolate Fabric traffic, and Azure Monitor for logs and alerts. Misconception: assuming cloud defaults are sufficient; you must explicitly choose disk types, replication, and networking topologies for Fabric workloads. Takeaway: plan storage IOPS, private networking, and monitoring before scaling to avoid performance surprises.

Use cloud volumes with appropriate IOPS and backups. Ledger growth needs predictable throughput.
Networking
Design private VPCs, subnets, and security groups; prioritize low-latency links for gossip and ordering traffic.

Integrate with cloud monitoring to track block times, endorsement latency, and storage metrics; alert on anomalies.

screens.title: Activity: Add Org3 and Verify peer0.org3
screens.narratorSegment: This activity guides you through adding Org3 using the test-network helper and verifying peer0. org3 has synchronized. Begin by bringing the test-network up with the CA enabled to ensure identity registration works. The commands are provided in the test-network; run./network. sh down then./network. sh up createChannel -ca to create mychannel with Org1 and Org2. Next, execute./addOrg3/addOrg3. sh up -c mychannel to generate Org3 crypto, update the channel config, and start the Org3 containers. After the script completes, verify Org3 appears in the channel config by fetching the config block as an Org1 admin, decoding it, and listing Application groups. You should see Org3MSP added. Then switch context to Org3 admin environment variables and fetch the genesis or latest block, run peer channel join -b mychannel. block, and wait for the gossip-based ledger sync. Use peer channel getinfo to confirm the block height matches peer0. org1 or peer0. org2. Finally, run a chaincode query such as GetAllAssets (if chaincode is installed) to confirm state. A common mistake is trusting the script without checking logs or block heights; always perform the verification steps and review container logs for errors. This activity demonstrates the full lifecycle from automation to manual verification required in production changes.

keyIdea.text: Run the addOrg3 script and manually verify Org3 appears in channel config, peer joins and catches up, and chaincode queries return expected results.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Hands-on: Add Org3
Starter steps
cd fabric-samples/test-network
./network.sh down
./network.sh up createChannel -ca
./addOrg3/addOrg3.sh up -c mychannel

# Verify Org3 in config
peer channel fetch config config_block.pb -o localhost:7050 --tls --cafile ...
configtxlator proto_decode --input config_block.pb --type common.Block --output config_block.json
jq '.data.data[0].payload.data.config.channel_group.groups.Application.groups | keys' config_block.json
Look for ["Org1MSP","Org2MSP","Org3MSP"] as confirmation.
Join and verify
# As Org3 Admin
export CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID="Org3MSP"
export CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH=.../Org3/users/Admin@org3.example.com/msp
export CORE_PEER_ADDRESS=localhost:11051
peer channel fetch 0 mychannel.block -o localhost:7050 --tls --cafile ...
peer channel join -b mychannel.block
peer channel getinfo -c mychannel
# Confirm block height matches other peers
peer chaincode query -C mychannel -n basic -c '{"Args":["GetAllAssets"]}'
Tip: if heights differ, inspect peer logs for block transfer issues and check gossip connectivity and TLS certs.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the core concepts to keep in mind. First, vertical scaling raises node capacity but can create single points of failure; use it for quick gains or for components that are hard to distribute. Second, horizontal scaling — adding peers, orderers, or CA instances — spreads load and increases resilience, but introduces synchronization, gossip, and consensus overhead that you must manage. Third, sharding with multiple channels partitions transaction load across independent ledgers to increase throughput when domains are separable, but it brings operational complexity and requires application-level handling for cross-channel workflows. Each of these ideas maps to operational practices: verify ledger synchronization after adding peers, perform channel config updates to change Raft membership, and provision persistent cloud storage with adequate IOPS. When planning cloud deployments, prioritize managed Kubernetes for orchestration, durable volumes for ledgers, secure networking, and integrated observability. These core concepts guide your scaling strategy so you can balance throughput, cost, and reliability in production Fabric networks.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this chapter you will learn how to make a Hyperledger Fabric network grow reliably as user demand and transaction volume increase. We begin with a practical distinction: vertical scaling means increasing C P U, memory, or disk for an existing node, while horizontal scaling means adding more peers, orderers, or CAs. Both approaches are useful; vertical scaling gives quick capacity gains but hits limits and can create single points of failure, while horizontal scaling favors resilience and distribution. You will see concrete steps for adding a peer to a channel and for expanding a Raft ordering cluster. We also cover sharding with multiple channels, which partitions workload so independent ledgers process transactions in parallel, and cloud deployment concerns such as persistent storage, managed Kubernetes, networking, and monitoring. A short hands-on activity shows the test-network addOrg3 script and the verification commands you will run. As you move through the lesson, notice trade-offs: throughput versus synchronization overhead, and resilience versus configuration complexity. By the end you should be able to choose where to invest resources, how to add instances safely, and how to design channels to increase throughput without breaking application semantics. Consider what would be harder to change later: a single oversized node or a channel design that prevents sharding? That question will guide your design choices.

In this segment we set clear, measurable objectives so you know what competence looks like. First, you will be able to distinguish between vertical and horizontal scaling strategies for each Fabric component and explain the trade-offs in terms of throughput, availability, and operational complexity. For example, you should be able to explain why a CA may remain a vertical candidate initially while peers are scaled horizontally. Second, you will learn how to implement horizontal scaling by adding peers and organizations to a running Fabric network. This includes registration with the CA, generating MSP materials, starting the new peer, and ensuring it joins channels and synchronizes its state database. Both objectives stress practical verification steps so you can show a new peer's block height matches existing peers. These skills matter because scaling decisions affect cost, resilience, and the ability to meet SLAs. Expect to practice these steps using the test-network scripts and to reason about when to choose vertical upgrades instead of adding instances. By the end you will have both the how-to steps and the judgement criteria for production deployments.

This second objectives slide focuses on operational outcomes and cloud readiness. First, you will understand how to scale the ordering service by adding Raft nodes, including why odd-numbered quorums matter and how adding nodes increases fault tolerance while raising consensus overhead. Second, you will be able to design channel-based sharding: decide when separate ledgers make sense, create channels for independent domains, and plan chaincode deployments per channel. Third, you will learn cloud-specific actions: how managed Kubernetes simplifies orchestration for containerized Fabric components, why persistent cloud volumes are required for ledgers and state DBs, and how to distribute nodes across availability zones for high availability and disaster recovery. Finally, you will identify common scaling mistakes — under-provisioned storage, ignoring network latency, and missing monitoring — and adopt preventive measures. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or diagram to help retention, and a verified milestone so you can demonstrate your operational competence in a real deployment, including verifying storage IOPS, pod distribution across zones, and alerting for latency spikes.

Let's define the two fundamental scaling axes and see what they mean for Fabric. Vertical scaling is increasing the resources of an existing server or container: more C P U cores, more R A M, faster disks. For a Fabric peer or orderer, vertical scaling raises single-node capacity, allowing heavier endorsement workloads or faster block processing on that node. However, vertical scaling eventually hits hardware or cost ceilings and concentrates risk: if that node fails, its services are unavailable unless other redundant nodes exist. Horizontal scaling is adding more instances of a component: more peers in an organization, additional orderers in a Raft cluster, or more CA replicas. In Fabric horizontal scaling distributes load and improves fault tolerance because requests can be balanced across instances. In practice, Fabric favors horizontal scaling where possible: peers can endorse and serve queries in parallel, Raft nodes can be added to tolerate failures, and multiple CAs can be deployed behind a load balancer. A common misconception is that simply adding peers will always increase throughput without costs: more peers increase gossip and state synchronization overhead and can add endorsement policy complexity. A concrete example: adding peer0. org3 to a channel spreads endorsement load for read-heavy queries, but you must ensure it synchronizes the ledger with existing peers before serving clients. Takeaway: match the axis to the component's role — use vertical improvements for input and output-bound storage or temporary boosts, and horizontal expansion for sustained, distributed demand.

Scaling peers means adding new instances so endorsement and query load distributes. The practical sequence has clear stages: identity provisioning, crypto material generation, container start, channel join, and verification. Start by registering and enrolling the new peer identity with your Fabric CA. That produces a cryptographic identity and MSP folder. Next, create or copy the peer's TLS artifacts and ensure the CORE_PEER_* environment variables describe the new instance. When the peer process starts, it advertises itself and participates in gossip. Before exposing it to clients, the peer must obtain the channel genesis or latest config block and run peer channel join. That causes the peer to request missing blocks from existing peers and sync its ledger via gossip. After joining, verify synchronization by running peer channel getinfo to compare block height to a known good peer. A concrete example: adding peer0. org3 to mychannel requires setting CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID to Org3MSP, pointing CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH to Org3 Admin MSP, and setting CORE_PEER_ADDRESS to the peer's endpoint, then running peer channel join -b mychannel. block. A common misconception is that a newly started peer will immediately serve queries; it will not reliably do so until its state database and ledger are synchronized. Final takeaway: follow the sequence and always verify block height and sample chaincode queries before routing production traffic.

We'll walk through the test-network addOrg3 script conceptually so you understand what it automates and what you should check afterwards. The addOrg3. sh script generates crypto material for the new organization, creates an Org3 definition file, updates the channel configuration to include the new organization, and starts the peer0. org3 and CLI containers. In practice, the script runs many discrete steps: it calls cryptogen or Fabric CA tooling to create MSP folders, it prepares a channel configuration delta to add Org3MSP as a member of the Application group, and it submits a config update transaction signed by an admin from an existing organization. After the config update is applied, the script starts the Org3 containers and often joins the peer to the channel automatically. When you run the script in a lab, verify three outcomes: first, that the new organization appears in the channel configuration keys; second, that peer0. org3 successfully joined the channel and synchronized its ledger; third, that any required chaincode is installed or that you can query the ledger from Org3. A common pitfall is assuming the script completed successfully without inspecting logs; always check the config fetch decode output or run jq on the decoded config to confirm Org3MSP presence. Final guidance: treat the script as a time-saver but keep manual verification steps in your deployment checklist.

Understanding gossip and ledger synchronization is essential when you add peers. Fabric's gossip protocol is the mechanism peers use to discover each other and replicate ledger blocks and state updates. When a new peer joins a channel it does not have the full ledger; it requests missing blocks after fetching the channel genesis or config block. Existing peers supply blocks through a combination of peer-to-peer block transfers and state transfer mechanisms. The new peer will replay those blocks to rebuild its chain and update its state database. A concrete example: after running peer channel join, the peer will query peers that have the blocks and receive them over the gossip protocol until its block height matches the channel. A common misconception is assuming ledger sync is instantaneous; large ledgers or slow network links can make synchronization take significant time, and peers must be monitored until their block height is consistent. Operationally, ensure the new peer has access to persistent storage sized for the ledger and that firewalls allow gossip ports. Key checks include peer channel getinfo to compare heights and performing a chaincode query to confirm expected state. Takeaway: gossip enables scaling peers but requires planning for synchronization time and network capacity to avoid false readiness assumptions.

Fabric's Raft ordering service is a crash-fault-tolerant consensus mechanism where ordering nodes form a cluster that provides block ordering and consensus. Horizontal scaling of Raft involves adding consenters (orderer nodes) to the cluster. A practical rule is to use an odd number of nodes — three, five, or seven — so the cluster can tolerate floor(n/2) failures while still achieving quorum. Adding nodes increases resilience: the cluster can survive more node failures without losing liveness. However, there is a trade-off: each additional node increases the communication and replication overhead required for consensus, which can affect latency, especially under high load. To add a Raft node you must generate its crypto material, fetch the latest channel config, add the new consenter entry to the config, and submit an update so other orderers accept the new member. After the config update, start the new orderer so it joins the cluster. Misconception to avoid: more orderers always improves throughput. In many cases the bottleneck is ordering throughput per channel and the increased consensus traffic can raise latency. A concrete example: expanding from three to five nodes increases tolerated failures from one to two, but you should test latency impacts. Takeaway: expand Raft to improve fault tolerance, but measure consensus overhead and align node count with your availability and latency requirements.

Adding a Raft orderer is an operational process with careful sequencing. Begin by generating the new orderer's cryptographic material — its TLS and MSP — using your chosen tooling. Next, fetch the latest channel configuration block from a trusted orderer and decode it to JSON. Prepare a config delta that adds the new consenter entry under the Orderer section, including its host, port, and TLS root certificate. Sign and submit the config update using the required administrative signatures from consenting organizations. After the network accepts the updated config, start the new orderer process with the generated crypto material so it can join the cluster and participate in leader election. Throughout this sequence, monitor logs for errors and confirm replication of blocks to the new node. Remember a practical misconception: you cannot simply point an orderer at an existing cluster and expect it to join without performing the channel config update; the cluster must explicitly include the new consenter. A sample conceptual command flow highlights the steps but not exact CLI syntax because implementations vary: generate crypto, fetch config, modify JSON to add consenter, create update envelope, sign and submit, then start orderer. Final takeaway: treat ordering changes as configuration surgery — prepare backups and validate cluster behavior under load after the change.

Certificate Authorities manage identities and are vital for secure operations. A single CA instance can serve many organizations in a small deployment, but for production you should plan for high availability and load balancing. Fabric CA servers support configuration in front of a load balancer and can share a database backend so multiple CA instances present a single logical service. When scaling CAs horizontally, ensure the backing database supports concurrent access and backups. Vertical scaling is sometimes used for a CA during quick growth to improve response times, but it leaves a central point of failure unless replicated. Practically, you might deploy multiple CA replicas behind a load balancer and use a managed database service that provides automated backups and multi-AZ redundancy. A misconception is treating CA scaling the same as peers: while peers replicate ledgers and can be added progressively, CA scaling requires careful handling of signing keys and database consistency. Example operational steps include configuring a shared database, deploying two or more CA instances with sticky sessions disabled, and verifying enrollment responses from different replicas. Takeaway: make CAs highly available with redundant instances and robust storage, and include CA health in your restoration playbook because identity data is critical for recovery.

Sharding in Fabric is achieved by using multiple channels, where each channel maintains its own independent ledger and ordering. This approach enables parallel transaction processing because transactions on one channel do not contend with those on another channel's ordering pipeline. The key to effective sharding is logical partitioning: identify domains or data sets that can operate independently. For example, a supply chain network can separate raw-material tracking and finished-goods distribution into different channels so each set of transactions is ordered and endorsed independently. Implementation requires careful design: which organizations join which channels, how chaincode is deployed per channel, and how client applications route transactions to the appropriate channel. A common pitfall is failing to plan for cross-channel workflows; Fabric does not provide native cross-channel chaincode invocation, so cross-domain interactions require off-chain coordination or specialized application logic. A concrete scenario: partition by geography — na-channel, eu-channel, asia-channel — then route transactions based on asset location. Benefits include increased overall throughput and reduced contention, but trade-offs are added operational complexity, more ledgers to manage, and potential data duplication. Takeaway: use channels as a sharding mechanism when domains are separable and design cross-channel interactions explicitly at the application layer.

Managed Kubernetes services simplify running containerized Fabric components by handling node lifecycle, service discovery, and many operational primitives. Using AKS, EKS, or GKE allows you to deploy peers, orderers, and CAs as pods, benefit from Kubernetes Services for internal traffic, and use Horizontal Pod Autoscalers for stateless components. However, Fabric components are stateful and need persistent volumes for ledgers and state databases. Plan for persistent volume claims with adequate IOPS and backup strategies. Also prepare node pools with appropriate VM sizes for C P U and memory needs, and use pod affinity or anti-affinity to distribute peers across availability zones. Managed Kubernetes also provides native integrations for logging and monitoring; connect Fabric logs to the cloud's monitoring stack for alerts on latency, block processing times, and storage utilization. A common misconception is that Kubernetes alone handles all scaling automatically; many Fabric components require manual configuration, persistent storage provisioning, and careful stateful set definitions. Example action items: define StatefulSets for peers with PVCs, configure NetworkPolicies to limit traffic to necessary ports, and use readiness probes that check block height or chaincode health. Takeaway: managed Kubernetes reduces operational burden but does not eliminate planning for persistent storage, network security, and stateful workload behavior.

When scaling Fabric in the cloud, persistent storage, networking, and monitoring are the three pillars that determine operational reliability. Persistent storage ensures ledger and state databases survive pod restarts and node failures; choose cloud volumes with the required IOPS and throughput, and plan for scheduled backups. Under-provisioned storage is a common cause of performance problems and needs capacity planning against expected ledger growth. Networking is critical: configure VPCs, subnets, and security groups so Fabric components communicate securely with minimal latency; gossip and ordering traffic needs low-latency links to avoid consensus slowdowns. High-availability demands distributing peers and orderers across availability zones and carefully setting network routing and firewall rules. Observability completes the picture: integrate Fabric logs and metrics into cloud monitoring solutions to surface block processing time, endorsement latency, and storage utilization. Without monitoring, bottlenecks can remain hidden until users are impacted. A practical example is using Azure AKS with managed disks for PVCs, network policies to isolate Fabric traffic, and Azure Monitor for logs and alerts. Misconception: assuming cloud defaults are sufficient; you must explicitly choose disk types, replication, and networking topologies for Fabric workloads. Takeaway: plan storage IOPS, private networking, and monitoring before scaling to avoid performance surprises.

This activity guides you through adding Org3 using the test-network helper and verifying peer0. org3 has synchronized. Begin by bringing the test-network up with the CA enabled to ensure identity registration works. The commands are provided in the test-network; run./network. sh down then./network. sh up createChannel -ca to create mychannel with Org1 and Org2. Next, execute./addOrg3/addOrg3. sh up -c mychannel to generate Org3 crypto, update the channel config, and start the Org3 containers. After the script completes, verify Org3 appears in the channel config by fetching the config block as an Org1 admin, decoding it, and listing Application groups. You should see Org3MSP added. Then switch context to Org3 admin environment variables and fetch the genesis or latest block, run peer channel join -b mychannel. block, and wait for the gossip-based ledger sync. Use peer channel getinfo to confirm the block height matches peer0. org1 or peer0. org2. Finally, run a chaincode query such as GetAllAssets (if chaincode is installed) to confirm state. A common mistake is trusting the script without checking logs or block heights; always perform the verification steps and review container logs for errors. This activity demonstrates the full lifecycle from automation to manual verification required in production changes.

Here are the core concepts to keep in mind. First, vertical scaling raises node capacity but can create single points of failure; use it for quick gains or for components that are hard to distribute. Second, horizontal scaling — adding peers, orderers, or CA instances — spreads load and increases resilience, but introduces synchronization, gossip, and consensus overhead that you must manage. Third, sharding with multiple channels partitions transaction load across independent ledgers to increase throughput when domains are separable, but it brings operational complexity and requires application-level handling for cross-channel workflows. Each of these ideas maps to operational practices: verify ledger synchronization after adding peers, perform channel config updates to change Raft membership, and provision persistent cloud storage with adequate IOPS. When planning cloud deployments, prioritize managed Kubernetes for orchestration, durable volumes for ledgers, secure networking, and integrated observability. These core concepts guide your scaling strategy so you can balance throughput, cost, and reliability in production Fabric networks.

Use this operational checklist as a memory aid when you perform scaling actions. First, always verify ledger synchronization after adding peers: compare block heights and run chaincode queries to ensure state matches. Second, for Raft changes back up configs and perform membership updates during maintenance windows; test the consensus behavior and measure latency after adding nodes. Third, in cloud deployments provision persistent volumes with required IOPS, configure network isolation and multi-AZ distribution, and integrate monitoring so you detect bottlenecks early. These operational reminders reduce risk and support a predictable scaling process for production Fabric networks. Key Concepts — Operational Checklist means verify sync, plan raft changes carefully, and provision storage, networking, and monitoring for cloud deployments..
